state.misconception_label: Believes f(x - a) translates the function up a units

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: What transformation maps the graph of \(y=f(x) \) to the graph of \( y=f(x-3) \). I got Translation by vector
\(
\left[\begin{array}{l}
0 \\
3
\end{array}\right]
\) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think of it this way: Imagine you have a playground with a slide that starts at point (0,0). If you move the slide to the right by 3 units, where will the starting point now be? This will help us see how the function \( f(x-3) \) shifts the graph of \( f(x) \) horizontally.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so if I move the slide to the right by 3 units, the starting point would be at (3,0)... but I'm still confused about why it's f(x-3) that makes it move right instead of left? Like, shouldn't minus mean it goes left?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think back to when we discussed misconceptions in reading from graphs. Just like how we had to focus on the y-value, in this case, we need to focus on the x-value. When we see f(x - 3), it means we're shifting the graph to the right by 3 units, not to the left. So, just like with the quadratic graph, we need to pay attention to the specific value being adjusted in the function.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher correctly identifies the student has both vertical/horizontal confusion and sign confusion, but responds with an analogy that doesn't address why the minus sign causes rightward movement, then in Turn 3 simply asserts the correct answer without explanation, leaving the student's core confusion unresolved.
score.justification_pass2: While Turn 1 uses a concrete playground slide analogy consistent with experiential teaching, Turn 3 abandons this approach entirely in favor of abstract rule-based reasoning about 'misconceptions' and 'specific values,' failing to ground the counterintuitive x-3 → right shift in any real-world experience.
